meta.label: Smartwatches and wearables
meta.attribution: Options are individual current models of smartwatch, fitness band and smart ring sold in the US, UK and EU (two open-source watches ship worldwide). Repairable: iFixit's smartwatch repairability table or device page (0 to 10, converted to 0 to 100) where the model has a score; where it has none, the score instead reflects the maker's own published repair route, a different kind of evidence noted in each cell: a maker battery service or parts programme scores around 40, a warranty that only swaps whole units and treats the battery as a consumable around 20, a sealed ring that cannot be opened 5. Battery life per charge: the maker's stated figure in normal smartwatch use, roughly 25 for under a day up to 95 for unlimited solar; frequent charging also wears a battery sooner. First-year cost: the maker's own US store price on the date checked, plus any membership the maker says the core experience needs (Oura's), scored as 100 minus one point per $10, floor 5; pounds are treated at par where a maker sells only in pounds. Health data handling: what each maker's privacy policy or security page says about selling data, advertising use, encryption and where data is stored, plus independent security findings (the US National Vulnerability Database and SySS for COROS). Mozilla's Privacy Not Included guide, once the usual reference here, was retired and could not be used. Works without the maker's app: whether the open-source Gadgetbridge project lists the device and how it pairs, whether the maker allows data export or an open firmware, and which phone the device requires. Not scored: sensor accuracy, which needs lab testing this catalogue cannot do, and software update promises, which most makers do not publish. Sources: ifixit.com, gadgetbridge.org, apple.com, store.google.com, support.google.com, samsung.com, garmin.com, ouraring.com, amazfit.com, coros.com, polar.com, pine64.com, espruino.com, nvd.nist.gov, syss.de. Not medical advice. Reviewed 2026-10. Suggest changes via Contribute.

reads.text: Compare smartwatches and wearables by repairability, support life, cost, and privacy.

axes.label: Cost or overall fit
axes.question: Lower cost or a stronger overall fit?

axes.label: Repair or lifespan
axes.question: Easier to open and fix, or longer before the battery gives out?

consumer.axes: Round 8 practical decision dials, with the S4 cost-or-values default where evidence permits.
consumer.budget: Round 8 honest budget eligibility, with S4 refusing to guess missing cost data.
consumer.archetypes: Round 8 computed answer slots matched to available category evidence.
consumer.page: Round 7 personal precedence extended in Round 9 to the shared decision page for every live category.

products.name: Apple Watch Series 12
products.description: Apple's mainstream smartwatch for iPhone owners, with strong health-data encryption but repairs only through Apple.

repairability.note: iFixit's smartwatch table scores the Series 12 (46 mm) 4 out of 10, one point up on the Series 10 thanks to battery pull tabs, and lists 'No official repair parts or instructions are available.' Apple's own out-of-warranty estimate is $99 for battery service.

longevity.note: Apple's comparison page lists up to 24 hours of battery life for the Series 12, or up to 38 hours in Low Power Mode, so it needs charging about daily; a battery that cycles daily wears faster.

economical.note: Apple's store lists the Series 12 from $399; no subscription is required for the core health features, so the first-year cost is the list price.

privacy.note: Apple says Health data synced to iCloud is end-to-end encrypted when two-factor authentication is on, and its iCloud security overview lists Health data among the end-to-end encrypted categories. Data still sits in an Apple account, which keeps this short of a device that needs no account.

openness.note: Apple's specs page says the Series 12, Ultra 4 and SE 3 require iPhone 11 or later with iOS 27 or later, so the watch cannot be used with Android or a third-party companion app; Apple is not among the watch vendors Gadgetbridge lists.

products.name: Apple Watch Ultra 4
products.description: Apple's rugged, larger watch with two-day battery life, the same Apple-only repair route and an iPhone requirement.

repairability.note: iFixit's smartwatch table gives the Ultra 4 4 out of 10; its October 2026 teardown says the Ultra 4 'is essentially the same as its predecessors' and that the only repair channel for Apple Watch is to take it back to Apple.

longevity.note: Apple lists up to 50 hours of battery life for the Ultra 4, or up to 84 hours in Low Power Mode, roughly double the Series 12.

economical.note: Apple's store lists the Ultra 4 from $799, with no required subscription for the watch itself.

privacy.note: Apple's health page says health data is encrypted on the device, and that with default two-factor authentication it is encrypted end-to-end so 'not even Apple can access your information'. The watch still depends on an Apple account.

openness.note: The Ultra 4 needs an iPhone 11 or later on iOS 27, per Apple's specs footnote; no Android pairing and no Gadgetbridge support.

products.name: Apple Watch SE 3
products.description: Apple's cheapest current watch, with the shortest battery life in the line-up and no iFixit score yet.

repairability.note: iFixit has not scored the SE 3, so this rests on a different kind of evidence: Apple's repair page offers battery service for out-of-warranty watches, and iFixit's 2026 teardown notes Apple sells no Watch repair parts or tools to independent or DIY repairers. Repair is possible only through Apple.

longevity.note: Apple's comparison page lists up to 18 hours for the SE 3, or 32 hours in Low Power Mode, the shortest of the three current models.

economical.note: Apple's store lists the SE 3 from $249, the lowest entry price in Apple's watch range.

privacy.note: The SE 3 uses the same Health app protections: Apple's iCloud data security overview lists Health data as end-to-end encrypted with keys held on trusted devices.

openness.note: Apple says the SE 3 requires an iPhone 11 or later; it cannot pair with Android phones or open companion apps.

products.name: Google Pixel Watch 5
products.description: Google's 2026 Wear OS watch, scored by iFixit as among the easiest smartwatches to repair, for Android phones only.

repairability.note: iFixit's smartwatch table gives the Pixel Watch 5 a provisional 9 out of 10 and says 'Google offers official repair parts and instructions'; screen, battery and band replacements are called the easiest of any smartwatch on the market.

longevity.note: Google's store page lists up to 30 hours for the 41 mm model and up to 40 hours for the 45 mm model, so it charges every day or two.

economical.note: The Google Store lists the Pixel Watch 5 from $399.99. Google Health Premium ($9.99 a month after a trial) is optional, so it is not added here.

privacy.note: Google's Google Health privacy FAQ says 'Google committed to not use Fitbit users' health and wellness data for Google Ads', and data is handled under a Google Account. Health data is still stored in Google's cloud, and the Fitbit privacy policy says Google never sells personal information.

openness.note: Google's store page says the watch works with most phones on Android 12 or newer and requires a Google Account and the Pixel Watch app; Google watches are not on Gadgetbridge's watch vendor list.

products.name: Google Pixel Watch 4
products.description: The 2025 Pixel Watch, the first to use screws and gaskets instead of glue, now sold at a lower price.

repairability.note: iFixit scores the Pixel Watch 4 9 out of 10. Its teardown says the battery comes out after 'Two more screws and one connector' and that the display is sealed with a replaceable O-ring gasket rather than adhesive.

longevity.note: Google lists 30 hours for the 41 mm watch and up to 40 hours for the 45 mm watch.

economical.note: The Google Store showed the Pixel Watch 4 from $249.99 on the date checked, a $200 saving on its list price; Google Health Premium is optional.

privacy.note: Google's privacy FAQ says Fitbit accounts can no longer be used after May 19, 2026, so health data sits in a Google Account, and it repeats its commitment not to use that health and wellness data for Google Ads.

openness.note: Requires an Android 11 or newer phone, a Google Account and the Pixel Watch app, per Google's store footnotes; no open companion app support.

products.name: Fitbit Charge 6
products.description: Google's slim fitness band, with a week of battery but a glued case that iFixit found hard to reseal.

repairability.note: iFixit's smartwatch table scores the Charge 6 4 out of 10: specialty tools are needed to pry up the display, and 'No official repair parts or instructions are offered.'

longevity.note: Google's store page says the Charge 6 can go for up to 7 days between charges.

economical.note: The Google Store lists the Charge 6 at $159.95; Google Health Premium is optional and not counted.

privacy.note: The Fitbit privacy policy (updated February 2026) says 'We never sell the personal information of our users', while also describing partners that serve advertisements for Fitbit's own marketing. Health data now lives in a Google Account.

openness.note: Google says the Charge 6 requires a compatible Android or iOS phone, a Google Account and internet access. Fitbit trackers are not on Gadgetbridge's watch vendor list.

products.name: Samsung Galaxy Watch Ultra (2025)
products.description: Samsung's rugged Wear OS watch, with a screwed back cover and gasket that iFixit rated well for repair.

repairability.note: iFixit's device page for the Galaxy Watch Ultra (the July 2024 model, listed in its smartwatch table as Galaxy Watch7 Ultra) shows a provisional 7 out of 10: the back cover unscrews and is sealed with a reusable gasket. Samsung sells the watch in 2026 as Galaxy Watch Ultra (2025); iFixit has not separately scored that edition.

longevity.note: Samsung's page cites up to 100 hours of battery in Power Saving Mode and 48 hours in Exercise Power Saving; typical use is lower.

economical.note: Samsung's US store listed the Galaxy Watch Ultra (2025) at $649.99 before trade-in credit on the date checked.

privacy.note: Samsung's US privacy policy says it uses personal data for personalized advertising and shares data with advertising service providers, with consent where required. That is broader data use than the health-only makers here.

openness.note: Samsung says the watch pairs with Android phones and that some features, such as ECG and sleep apnea detection, are unavailable with non-Samsung Android phones. No Gadgetbridge support and no iPhone pairing.

products.name: Samsung Galaxy Ring
products.description: Samsung's screenless health-tracking ring; light to wear but, like all current smart rings, impossible to open.

repairability.note: iFixit's CT-scan teardown calls the Galaxy Ring 100% disposable because 'you can't get to the battery without destroying the device in the process'. There is no repair route once the battery wears out.

longevity.note: Samsung says the ring lasts up to 7 days on a charge for sizes 12 and 13 and up to 6 days for smaller sizes, and the charging case extends that to about 14 days away from an outlet.

economical.note: Samsung's ring page lists the Galaxy Ring from $299.99 before trade-in, with no required subscription.

privacy.note: The ring syncs through Samsung Health and a Samsung account; Samsung's US privacy policy allows personalized advertising with consent and sharing with advertising service providers.

openness.note: Gadgetbridge's ring section covers Amazfit, Ultrahuman and Colmi rings but not Samsung's, so the Galaxy Ring needs Samsung's own apps.

products.name: Garmin Forerunner 570
products.description: A running watch with an AMOLED screen and about 11 days of battery, which open-source Gadgetbridge can pair without Garmin's app.

repairability.note: iFixit has not scored a current Garmin watch (its only Garmin entry, the Venu Sq, scored 3 out of 10). This rests on Garmin's own US limited warranty, which excludes batteries as consumable parts and says Garmin may replace a device with a new or Garmin Recertified one; Garmin publishes no parts or battery service.

longevity.note: Garmin's product page advertises up to 11 days of battery in smartwatch mode.

economical.note: Garmin's US store listed the Forerunner 570 at $549.99 on the date checked; no subscription is required.

privacy.note: Garmin's global privacy policy answers its own question about whether Garmin sells personal data with a plain no: it does not sell personal data to anyone. Data is stored in a Garmin account by default.

openness.note: Gadgetbridge lists the Forerunner 570 as mostly supported, with initial pairing possible 'without needing the proprietary vendor app', so it can be used without a Garmin account.

products.name: Garmin Venu 4
products.description: Garmin's lifestyle and health smartwatch, with roughly ten days per charge.

repairability.note: No iFixit score for the Venu 4. Garmin's consumer limited warranty treats batteries as consumables, and warranty remedies are repair, replacement with a recertified unit, or refund at Garmin's option; there is no published owner battery replacement.

longevity.note: Garmin's US product page lists up to 10 days of battery life in smartwatch mode.

economical.note: Listed at $549.99 on Garmin's US store when checked, no subscription needed.

privacy.note: Garmin's privacy policy states it does not sell personal data and shares it only in specific situations it lists, such as service providers and legal requests.

openness.note: Gadgetbridge rates the Venu 4 mostly supported, with no-vendor pairing, meaning it can sync to an open-source Android app instead of Garmin Connect.

products.name: Garmin Instinct 3 Solar
products.description: A rugged outdoor watch whose solar models can run indefinitely in smartwatch mode with enough daylight.

repairability.note: Garmin's warranty excludes batteries as consumable parts unless a defect caused the damage, and Garmin repairs or swaps devices at its option; no parts, manuals or iFixit score exist for the Instinct 3.

longevity.note: Garmin's launch release says AMOLED models get up to 24 days in smartwatch mode while 'the solar charging models can get unlimited battery life' in that mode, given enough sun.

economical.note: Garmin's launch release gives suggested retail prices starting at $399.99 for the solar models and $449.99 for AMOLED; the solar price is used here.

privacy.note: Instinct 3 data goes to Garmin Connect, covered by Garmin's privacy policy that says Garmin does not sell personal data.

openness.note: Gadgetbridge lists Instinct 3 and Instinct 3 Solar as mostly supported with pairing that needs no Garmin app.

products.name: Oura Ring 5
products.description: Oura's 2026 smart ring, smaller than the Ring 4, whose full app experience needs a paid membership.

repairability.note: Oura's warranty FAQ lists 'Consumable parts, including batteries' among things not covered, and iFixit's smart ring teardown notes a ring cannot be opened without destroying it. When the battery wears out the ring is replaced, not repaired.

longevity.note: Oura's store page says the Ring 5 gets 6 to 9 days of battery life.

economical.note: Oura's store lists the Ring 5 at $399 (silver), and membership costs $69.99 a year in the US. Oura's help centre says without a membership you see only three daily scores, so the membership is counted: about $469 in year one.

privacy.note: Oura's privacy policy says it does not use sensitive personal information for targeted advertising and does not sell or share personal information for cross-context behavioral advertising. Its membership page adds that Oura will never share data without consent.

openness.note: Oura's help centre says you can export all of your data in CSV format even without a membership, but the Oura API needs an active membership; Oura rings are not supported by Gadgetbridge.

products.name: Amazfit Balance 2
products.description: Zepp Health's mid-range smartwatch with three weeks of battery and strong Gadgetbridge support.

repairability.note: No iFixit score. Amazfit's US warranty excludes normal wear and tear, and its remedy is to repair or replace the device at Amazfit's option, possibly with a remanufactured unit; it publishes no parts or battery service.

longevity.note: Amazfit's US store page lists up to 21 days of battery life.

economical.note: Listed at $299.99 on Amazfit's US store when checked; Zepp's paid tier is optional.

privacy.note: Amazfit's privacy policy says 'We do not sell any personal information to third parties', but also that data is stored on servers of third-party providers and may move across jurisdictions, and it describes SSL for data in transit rather than end-to-end encryption.

openness.note: Gadgetbridge rates the Balance 2 highly supported, but pairing first requires the Zepp app to obtain an authentication key, so the vendor account is needed once.

products.name: Amazfit Bip 6
products.description: A low-cost AMOLED smartwatch from Zepp Health, the cheapest mainstream option here.

repairability.note: Covered by the same Amazfit limited warranty: repair or replacement at Amazfit's option, normal wear excluded, no parts or repair guides published, and no iFixit score.

longevity.note: Amazfit's US store page lists up to 14 days of battery life for the Bip 6.

economical.note: Amazfit's US store listed the Bip 6 at $79.99 when checked.

privacy.note: Zepp Health's US privacy policy says it does not sell personal information and stores data with third-party service providers worldwide; the policy promises reasonable safeguards but no end-to-end encryption of health data.

openness.note: Gadgetbridge lists the Bip 6 as highly supported, after a one-time key is pulled from the Zepp app.

products.name: COROS PACE 4
products.description: A light running watch with long battery life and a published flat-fee battery repair programme.

repairability.note: No iFixit score. COROS's Repair Program page lists a $59 battery repair for the PACE 4 ($79 for screen, dial or button) and says devices remain eligible for up to three years after the warranty ends; in practice COROS ships a refurbished unit.

longevity.note: COROS's PACE 4 page cites up to 19 days of daily use and 41 GPS hours.

economical.note: COROS's US store listed the PACE 4 at $249.00 when checked.

privacy.note: The US National Vulnerability Database record CVE-2025-32879 (June 2025) says none of the PACE 3's Bluetooth services required any authentication, so an attacker in range could configure or reset the watch or install software. SySS, which found it, lists the issue as fixed by COROS in mid-2025 and says other models might be affected. COROS's privacy policy says US users' data is stored on US servers.

openness.note: COROS is not among the watch vendors on Gadgetbridge's gadget list, so syncing needs the COROS app and account.

products.name: Polar Vantage M3
products.description: A Finnish multisport watch whose battery Polar's own service centre can replace.

repairability.note: No iFixit score. Polar's support page lists the Vantage M3 among devices whose battery 'can only be replaced at the Polar Central Service', so a worn battery is fixed rather than the watch thrown away, though not by the owner.

longevity.note: Polar's product page says the Vantage M3 runs up to 7 days in normal use.

economical.note: Polar's US store lists the Vantage M3 at $499.99.

privacy.note: Polar's privacy notice says it does not disclose, give or sell user data unless required by law, and that data is stored on Polar ecosystem servers in the EU/EEA area.

openness.note: Gadgetbridge's Polar page covers only Polar's H9 and H10 heart-rate sensors, not its watches, so the M3 relies on Polar's own app.

products.name: PINE64 PineTime
products.description: A very cheap open-source smartwatch for tinkerers, running community firmware with no account or cloud.

repairability.note: No iFixit score. PINE64's store sells the sealed PineTime with a 30-day warranty and no spare parts; an unsealed development kit at the same price can be opened, and the hardware is fully documented on the PINE64 wiki.

longevity.note: PINE64's wiki describes 'a week-long battery'; real life depends on the firmware you run.

economical.note: PINE64's store lists the sealed PineTime at a community price of $26.99 (retail $34.99).

privacy.note: The PineTime runs open firmware and needs no maker account; PINE64 describes it as community driven, 'allowing you to keep control of your device'. Data stays on the watch and the phone app you choose.

openness.note: PINE64 calls the PineTime 'a free and open source smartwatch capable of running custom-built open operating systems', and Gadgetbridge also pairs it without any vendor app.

products.name: Bangle.js 2
products.description: An open, hackable JavaScript smartwatch from UK maker Espruino, with about a month per charge.

repairability.note: No iFixit score. Espruino publishes its own disassembly guide, which involves heating the screen free and gluing it back with phone-screen adhesive on reassembly: documented by the maker, but not easy.

longevity.note: Espruino's page says 'you can expect around 1 month of battery life' with a once-a-minute clock on current firmware.

economical.note: Espruino's page lists the Bangle.js 2 from £83. Pounds are treated at par with dollars for this score, a rough simplification.

privacy.note: Espruino's page says you can install new apps from the web over Bluetooth, with no maker cloud in between, and Gadgetbridge pairs the watch directly without a vendor app.

openness.note: Espruino describes it as 'an open, hackable smartwatch' you can program in JavaScript, and Gadgetbridge rates it highly supported with no vendor app needed.
